content: Palliative care units are being established in 14 district hospitals within the public healthcare system to provide support to staff at primary healthcare (PHC) centers. The success of this initiative can be attributed to several factors, including advocacy by local non-governmental organizations (NGOs) emphasizing the importance of caring for chronically and terminally ill individuals from impoverished backgrounds. This advocacy has led to significant community involvement and political commitment from the state government. Additionally, the state government has implemented policies integrating palliative care into PHC, allocated funding for palliative care nurses in PHC centers, and leveraged Kerala’s decentralized governance system to empower local governments. The program also utilizes nurses and home care leaders to deliver care effectively. Access to essential controlled medicines, such as strong opioids like morphine, is critical for managing pain associated with cancer, HIV/AIDS, severe illnesses, traumatic injuries, burns, and surgeries. Despite being listed on the World Health Organization (WHO) Model List of Essential Medicines, morphine is often unavailable in sufficient quantities, appropriate dosage forms, or at an affordable price. Globally, 75% of the population lacks access to morphine or other strong opioids when clinically indicated for pain management. Each year, 5 million terminal cancer patients and 1 million end-stage HIV/AIDS patients suffer from untreated moderate to severe pain. International drug regulatory bodies, such as the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB), have historically focused on preventing opioid misuse and abuse rather than ensuring their medical availability. However, the United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs mandates that nations balance minimizing the risk of opioid abuse with ensuring their availability for medical and scientific purposes. This principle, known as the principle of balance, has been endorsed by WHO, the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs, and the United Nations General Assembly. While the misuse of controlled substances poses societal risks, regulatory systems should not create barriers to their legitimate medical use. Supply chain failures, such as stockouts, can lead to patient suffering, withdrawal symptoms, and increased risks of illicit opioid use and suicide. The Single Convention requires countries to report annual opioid consumption to the INCB, which uses this data to estimate global opioid needs and allocate appropriate quantities. Integrating palliative care into public health systems strengthens healthcare performance, reduces costs, and promotes universal health coverage (UHC). Palliative care networks, which include home care linked to hospital-based inpatient and outpatient units, not only improve patients’ quality of life but also reduce hospital stays and unnecessary admissions for symptom management, particularly near the end of life. This integration alleviates hospital overcrowding, reduces healthcare costs, and provides financial protection for patients and their families. Within hospitals, palliative care units can improve quality of life and reduce costs by minimizing the use of life-sustaining treatments and non-beneficial interventions, such as chemotherapy near the end of life. Although no studies from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) have been reported, integrating palliative care into healthcare systems may yield long-term benefits by improving patient outcomes, reducing healthcare costs, and addressing the overuse of hospitals. Specifically, integrating palliative care into PHC systems can expand home care services, particularly through community health workers (CHWs) and nurses. Home visits provide opportunities to assess household well-being, educate families, and promote early recognition of diseases like tuberculosis and cancer. These visits also address social issues such as food insecurity, lack of education, and inadequate housing. By doing so, palliative care integration strengthens health promotion, disease prevention, and early disease detection within PHC systems. Palliative home care visits can also improve adherence to outpatient treatments for conditions such as breast cancer, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, hypertension, and diabetes. These visits help prevent loss to follow-up for patients and their families receiving palliative care. Ministries of health and healthcare planners can estimate palliative care needs using resources like the WHO Global Atlas of Palliative Care and the Lancet Commission report on palliative care and pain relief. However, locally generated data is essential for accurately characterizing population health needs and informing healthcare planning. Reliable data helps prioritize investments in healthcare resources and optimize the benefits of palliative care integration into PHC. To design effective palliative care services, it is important to understand the suffering experienced by target populations, including physical, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions. Data collection should ideally involve direct input from patients, as their perspectives provide valuable insights. However, concise surveys, such as the Palliative Outcomes Scale, can be used to gather information from patients who may be unable to participate in lengthy surveys. Understanding local attitudes toward disability, suffering, dying, and death is also crucial for developing culturally appropriate palliative care services. Ongoing data collection on palliative care integration, accessibility, quality, and outcomes is essential for continuous improvement. WHO recommends health technology assessments (HTAs) to evaluate the impact of health interventions systematically. HTAs consider both intended and unintended consequences of interventions, informing policy decisions and resource allocation. For example, HTAs can assess the cost-effectiveness of integrating palliative care into PHC systems and identify interventions that provide the greatest health benefits and value for money. All palliative care providers, regardless of the care setting, should commit to continuous quality improvement. Data from quality indicators can guide service enhancements. Indicators for assessing national or regional palliative care programs include the existence of national policies, the availability of essential medicines like oral morphine, and the proportion of communities providing palliative care services. Additionally, new research concepts, such as extended cost-effectiveness analysis (ECEA) and suffering-adjusted life years (SALYs), can provide valuable insights into the impact of palliative care policies on patients and families. Finally, exploring the knowledge and attitudes of PHC providers and CHWs regarding palliative care can inform training programs and improve access to care. For instance, primary care physicians often fail to identify palliative care needs early in the course of life-limiting illnesses. Understanding the reasons for this delay can enhance access to palliative care. Self-assessments of competencies in addressing social, spiritual, and legal issues can also support the development of targeted training programs for CHWs and other healthcare providers.
